blocks.text: PART 9: THE TRUTH HE FINALLY HAD TO HEAR
Two weeks passed before Graham and I agreed to meet.
The meeting took place in Jonah’s office.
I wore a simple navy dress and carried a folder containing the documents I needed.
I had not worn any of the jewelry Graham had given me.
When he entered, I noticed that he looked different.
For a moment, I almost reached for his hand.
He seemed to be searching for something familiar.
Jonah reviewed the documents and explained the next steps.
Graham listened, but his attention kept returning to me.
When the formal discussion ended, Jonah excused himself.
“You should have considered me before it reached that point.”
For the first time, he didn’t immediately defend himself.
He had mistaken my patience for permanent permission.
He had believed that because I had forgiven him before, I would always forgive him.
He had believed that because I had adjusted to his habits, I would continue adjusting forever.
He had believed that because I loved him, I would tolerate anything.
“You used to come home exhausted, and I would wait up for you.”
“At some point, you stopped doing that.”
“You started treating me like another responsibility.”
“When I got sick, you left the bedroom.”
“When I wanted to hold your hand, you sometimes pulled away because you hadn’t washed up.”
“When I asked you to share a quiet evening with me, you said you were exhausted.”
“And suddenly you could share your food.”
“You could hold someone for hours without worrying about whether they had touched something you didn’t want to touch.”
“It made me feel as though there was something wrong with me.”
“I began questioning whether I was attractive enough, interesting enough, patient enough, or easy enough to love.”
“I spent years believing that if I understood your boundaries well enough, you would eventually feel comfortable being close to me.”
“But you were comfortable being close to someone else.”
For several seconds, neither of us spoke.
“You were busy being a wonderful surgeon to everyone else.”
“But you forgot to be a husband at home.”
I had seen Graham cry only twice before.
And once when he thought he had lost a patient during an operation.
I had always believed his tears meant something important.
“I want a husband who doesn’t need another woman to remind him how to be affectionate.”
“I want someone who doesn’t treat love like a set of rules that only apply to me.”
“I have given you eleven years of chances.”
“I don’t want to spend another year waiting for you to decide that I deserve the same kindness you give everyone else.”
But I no longer confused pity with love.
“But I know I cannot return to the way things were.”
“Please don’t make a final decision today.”
“Graham, I made this decision long before I boarded that plane.”
“The plane was simply the day I stopped postponing it.”
For the first time, he seemed to understand that my departure had not been an impulsive act.
It had been the final step in a decision that had taken months to make.
“Was there ever a moment when I could have stopped this?”
“You didn’t need to make a grand gesture.”
